stories.body:
What comes after the dissolution of the liberal world order.

Alden Young is an associate professor of history and global affairs at Yale University. He was a 2021-22 Berggruen Institute Fellow.

Muez Ali is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University in Qatar and honorary research fellow at University College London.

This work is supported by the Cross-Border Conflict Evidence, Policy and Trends (XCEPT) research program, funded by UK International Development. The views and opinions expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the UK government.

Sudan has often served as a mirror for judging the health of the liberal world order because it has repeatedly been a laboratory for multilateral interventions to prevent atrocities and stabilize the humanitarian situation.

During the second Sudanese civil war, which stretched from 1983 to 2005, an estimated more than two million people died. In Darfur during the first decade of the 2000s, international observers estimated that 300,000 people died and another 2-3 million people were displaced.

At the time, finding a solution to Sudan’s conflicts was a priority for the United States and the coalitions it galvanized. For instance, Sudan’s second civil war came to an end only after intense mediation by the troika of the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway, as well as Sudan’s African neighbors, in 2005. The level of Western concern and diplomatic resources mobilized to intervene in Sudan’s conflicts in the early 2000s feels almost unimaginable today.

In the 2000s, Sudan hosted two massive UN peacekeeping missions : the more than 13-year-long African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur, which ended in 2020 and the more than six-year-long United Nations Mission in the Sudan, which ended in 2011. The goals of these missions were to prevent genocide in Darfur and to guarantee the implementation of the peace agreement ending the civil war between the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement/Army and the government in Khartoum. This mission, which included approximately 10,000 soldiers and numerous civilian authorities, ended with a referendum on the independence of South Sudan in 2011. A few months later South Sudan was welcomed by the international community as the newest country in the world.

It was in this context — of the international efforts to end Sudan’s civil wars and the resulting mass displacements — that South Sudanese diplomat Francis Mading Deng developed the idea of “ sovereignty as responsibility .” Deng served as the Special Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General on internally displaced persons from 1992 to 2004, and many experts credit Deng’s idea of sovereignty as responsibility as the intellectual genesis of the international principle of the Responsibility to Protect . The UN General Assembly’s adoption of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principles in 2005 marked a high-water point for the legitimacy of the liberal world order. R2P, as formulated by Deng and others, tried to balance sovereignty as a state’s right to non-interference with the international community’s duty to ensure that a state protects the welfare of its own citizens.

Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm. The numbers are massive and stark, making it hard to comprehend the magnitude of the tragedy unfolding there. At least 14 million people have been internally displaced since the latest round of fighting in April 2023, according to the United Nations Refugee Agency. Meanwhile, there are at least 4.4 million Sudanese refugees who have fled the country, many to neighboring countries like Chad, Egypt and South Sudan, which can ill-afford to support this influx. Three years on, intense fighting persists in Sudan’s central region of Kordofan, in Darfur and in its southeastern Blue Nile state.

In one of the most widely discussed recent commentaries on the crisis in Sudan — a conflict often overshadowed despite its horrific violence by other wars — the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum wrote that “no statistics can express the sense of pointlessness, of meaninglessness, that the war has left behind” after she reported from behind the lines of both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and their opponents, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In the face of the physical destruction of cities like Khartoum, Applebaum declared the conflict the most nihilistic on Earth, writing with a tinge of hopelessness that “the liberal world order has already ended in Sudan, and there isn’t anything to replace it.”

In many ways, what is happening in Sudan represents the international community’s abandonment of the longstanding principles of the liberal world order, particularly by the West. Instead, Sudan has become the plaything for a wide array of actors stretching across the Middle East and Africa, to Russia and Ukraine, and as far afield as Colombia. After the Trump administration’s cuts to organizations like the U.S. Agency for International Development, even the commitment to prevent the spread of famine has declined. Applebaum ended her piece by lamenting that Sudan is now a victim of an anarchic, post-American world. A world that has yet to fully take shape in which “colonialism is long past, the Cold War has ended,” and the international order has irreparably broken down.

“Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm.”

But what is taking place in Sudan and elsewhere is not the emergence of anarchy; it is a return to precolonial patterns. Many observers have mistakenly assumed the former because of what the historian Richard Reid calls the “ foreshortening of African history ,” by which he means “the detachment of Africa’s turbulent present — and its recent past — from deeper patterns of both change and continuity.” Perhaps no country has suffered more from the reification of the colonial past by social scientists and modernizing elites alike than the Congo, once known as Zaire.

At the end of the 19th century, Henry Morten Stanley earned the name Bula Matari or the breaker of rocks, for “his feat of driving a caravan of porters bearing dismantled steamers over the torturous terrain between the Zaire River estuary and the vast navigable watercourses extending inward from Kinshasa.” As Zala Lusibu N’Kanza, the first woman to hold the position of minister in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, notes, “for all Bakongo the name of Bula Matari signified terror.” The precolonial was smashed in the wake of an ascendant and modernizing colonial and post-colonial state. For the founding generation of American political scientists like the late Crawford Young, the political, economic and social institutions of the precolonial period were left in ruins because they lacked the resilience to create an alternative to the modernizing state.

A Return To The Pre-Colonial Era

Despite the depths of the human tragedy playing out across northeast Africa — engulfing not only Sudan but South Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia and Somaliland — Applebaum’s post-American world is not just chaos. Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era. The long dominance of the colonial state was not the result of smashing African societies, as American political scientists long suspected. Just as the chaos marring the post-colonial period is not a result of ethnic rivalries. Rather, the endurance of colonialism in countries like Sudan is a product of the legacies of its infrastructure.

The peculiar durability of the infrastructure built during European control of the Nile basin resulted from a set of historical conjunctures. In his new book, “The Alibi of Capital: How We Broke the Earth to Steal the Future on the Promise of a Better Tomorrow,” the political theorist Timothy Mitchell argues that around the turn of the 20th century a new ability to discount the future was invented. Mitchell considers this ability a political technology “derived from the fact that time can be controlled — by the construction of a political apparatus that will reliably capture and colonize the future.” While this sounds incredibly abstract, Mitchell goes on to explain that:

“That the scale and extension of transportation lines and energy networks, along with urban development, irrigation projects, and other immense schemes, depended not just on material durability but upon the durable arrangements of law, authority, compulsion, and justification.”

Sudan, though often imagined as a colonial backwater, was the site of one of the British Empire’s largest investments in industrial agriculture ever. The giant Gezira irrigated agricultural scheme, one of the only monuments to colonialism visible from outer space, was originally planned in the 1920s to irrigate more than a million acres. British officials spoke openly of the Gezira Scheme’s potential to be a second man-made Nile Delta, a giant cotton farm for the Empire. From the 1920s until the scheme ran into financial problems in the 1970s, the railways, dams, ports and even Sudan’s labor force were geared to serve this project, not to mention the country’s financial and economic infrastructure.

This changed in the 1990s as the oil sector rose to prominence, but even then, pipelines and refineries tended to be located according to patterns established during the colonial era. These patterns endured in part because irrigation canals and railways cut into the earth and were reinforced with steel, and because Sudan integrated into global financial markets through loans for investments backed by access to export markets. Originally, it was cotton, later crude oil and now gold.

The Fragile Liberal International Order

When the Princeton political scientist G. John Ikenberry wrote about the liberal international order, he remarked that, “there is an optimist assumption lurking in liberal internationalism that states can overcome constraints and cooperate to solve security dilemmas, pursue collective action, and create an open, stable system.” Yet Ikenberry also admits that the system’s collective nature was always more aspirational than practical. Ikenberry admits that since 1945 the United States has served as the owner and operator of this system and has been afforded special privileges and responsibilities. Applebaum describes the chaos that unfolds in Sudan once the United States is no longer willing to bear its historic burden. Read Noema in print.

“Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era.”

But what if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable? While cotton and crude petroleum are different commodities, the central state could largely control their export, either by managing production directly or by issuing licenses for production and sale to favored clients. The boom in gold exports from Sudan since 2013 is remarkable because of the state’s utter inability to control the trade. For Sudan, the tragedy is magnified by the almost 200% rise in gold prices during that period, meaning the Sudanese state lost out on this windfall due to incapacity and now war. Part of the challenge for Sudanese authorities is that artisanal gold production , unlike control of oilfields and pipelines or cotton irrigation, lacks the central infrastructural chokepoints the colonial and postcolonial state had become so adept at taxing.

The other dilemma for the Sudanese state is the regional collapse of the taboo against dealing with subnational actors. As a result, gold from the mines of Darfur often ends up in the souks of Dubai without ever passing through the central government. Similarly, Sudanese soldiers guarding the Saudi-Yemeni border can be hired and deployed without ever contracting with the SAF. The RSF, a paramilitary-slash-merchant company, carries out many of these transactions, managing large portions of Sudan on behalf of its investors.

Precolonial Patterns Return In Contemporary Guises

What looks like chaos reveals patterns. In the 3 ½ years since fighting broke out between the SAF and the RSF, new trade and military supply routes have become increasingly visible. During the first few decades following Sudan’s independence in 1956, most economic activity flowed from the provinces to Khartoum, then along the railroad lines to Port Sudan on the Red Sea. The government earned most of its revenue by taxing the imports and exports that followed this well-trodden route. During the first two years of fighting, the Rapid Support Forces controlled Khartoum and did everything in their power to break the old colonial trade route. During this time, Sudan’s government retreated to Port Sudan, and the RSF set up a rival capital in Nyala in southern Darfur.

Inadvertently, the war revealed older patterns of state formation from the 19th century. Sudan’s city of Suakin and its other Red Sea ports claimed allegiance to a distant Ottoman government and resisted incorporation into the Kingdom of Sennar, to say nothing of Darfur. Elites in Suakin often sought incorporation into the Ottoman province of the Hijaz or Aden on the Arabian Peninsula. This pattern threatened to repeat itself when Sudan’s government was again temporarily forced to relocate to Port Sudan after Khartoum fell in 2023.

But perhaps more dramatically, the war saw the re-emergence of old trade routes to the north, west and south of Darfur. With the SAF in control of Port Sudan, the RSF began to turn to the old trade routes across the desert, the most famous of which was the Darb El Arba’īn, or “40 Day Road,” leading from northern Darfur to Asyut in southern Egypt. Other trade routes led north into Libya, where the RSF is suspected to have established bases under the protection of the Libyan militia leader who rules the eastern part of the country, Khalifa Haftar. Similarly, the trading routes from southern Darfur into South Sudan have been reactivated to resupply the RSF. These routes often end in Uganda, Kenya and the Central African Republic. All outside the control of the center.

The new prominence of the old trade routes was capped by the declaration of TASIS , or the Sudan Founding Alliance, of a new government in April 2025, exactly two years after the outbreak of the war. Speaking from Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, TASIS leaders tried to solidify an alliance between the RSF, parts of the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), a militant group and political party, and the leadership of the Baggara confederation. The Baggara includes more than six million Arab and African people stretching from southern Kordofan to Lake Chad.

The RSF’s organization, founded in 2013 — with the Darfurian Arab family of its leader Muhammad Hamdan Daglo Musa at its center — itself echoes an episode from the late 19th century. The first is the creation of a private-merchant empire by al-Zubayr Rahma al-Mansur, usually known as Zubayr Pasha . Originally a lackluster merchant assistant for an Egyptian trader, by the 1860s Zubayr had established one of the largest merchant companies operating in what we today refer to as South Sudan.

His operations were described in a remembrance in the “Middle East Monitor” as such: “[He sent] men ‘through the lands of the Dinka, Jur and Bongo, the company reached the Golo, then living between the Kuru and Kpongo rivers.’ They purchased ostrich feathers and ivory for trade in Khartoum, Cairo and beyond.” By the 1870s, he had grown from a successful trader into the ruler of a territory often called Deim Zubayr, controlling a large area of present-day South Sudan’s Bahr al-Ghazal and Darfur with an army of some 12,000 soldiers, many of whom were enslaved. According to the historian Tsega Etefa , writing in the Journal of Oromo Studies:

“What if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable?”

“By the late 1860s, al Zubayr was ‘the most prominent and successful of the merchant princes operating in the Bahr al-Ghazal.’ He traded in slaves and ivory; however, antislavery movements by Egyptian and European explorers in the Nile Valley began to put pressure on him. Therefore, ‘he arranged with the Baqqara tribes of southern Darfur for his slave caravans to pass through their territory northward, bypassing the Nile.’ Toward the end of the 1860s, ‘he attained the position of practically an independent ruler.’ The Egyptian government’s expeditionary force ‘was completely defeated by him, and the Egyptian authorities, realizing with what a commanding character they were confronted, made him Governor of the district.’”

Initially, Zubayr’s base was in the southern borderlands between Darfur and Bahr al-Ghazal. Darfur, as an independent political entity, was not conquered until 1874, when Zubayr’s forces achieved what the Ottoman-Egyptian armies of Muhammad Ali had been unable to do in 1821: conquering the Fur Sultanate at its capital of El Fasher. The parallels with the RSF appear to write themselves. These became particularly notable when the RSF took El Fasher after months of siege at the end of October 2025. In the process, the RSF captured the last major stronghold in Darfur and solidified their ability to resupply to the north through Libya and to the south across the expanse of South Sudan into East Africa.

Yet another echo of the 19th century was the emergence of Kordofan as a contested region. The armies of Muhammad Ali, de facto ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, partially pacified the region in the decades after the 1821 invasion from Egypt, but could not maintain stable control. In many ways, this resembles the situation in Kordofan today, where cities like El-Obeid , with a population over 600,000, remain under frequent attack as rival forces contend to dominate the region. Still, the 19th-century echoes perhaps become clearest in the relative autonomy of the SPLM-N, a political party and militant group with its strongholds based in southern Kordofan.

The SPLM-N has been both a broker and spoiler for South Sudan since its secession in 2011. The flat plains were easily conquered, but the Nuba Mountains were very difficult to ultimately control. One faction, SPLM-N Al-Hilu, which mostly controls the areas around the Nuba Mountains in South Kordofan, sided with the RSF, while another faction, SPLM-N Agar, which controls parts of the Blue Nile state, has sided with the SAF.

In the process, the two groups have maintained the autonomy of the border regions between the RSF, SAF and South Sudan. A borderland organization more interested in preserving its own autonomy than in the outcome of the war has found itself operating on both sides of the conflict. In this way, they are implementing strategies with other surprising parallels in the past, such as the Kingdom of Taqali , a kingdom in the northeastern Nuba Mountains of Sudan that flourished between about 1780 and 1884, with relative autonomy that extended well into Sudan’s post-independence period until 1969.

Our research in the Sudan Collection at the University of Bergen in Norway shows that during the 19th century, Taqali leaders used a similar strategy of seeking protection and recognition from both the waning states of Darfur and Sennar — pledging vassalage to both simultaneously as they worked to maintain autonomy.

The breakdown of the Sudanese state we are witnessing today is also not random. Rather, along with the retreat of the liberal world order, we are witnessing the reappearance of political orders that last manifested themselves with such clarity in the 19th century. These patterns repeat because they are based on trade and political and economic linkages that do not rely on the infrastructure built during the colonial period. The durability of this infrastructure has decayed as the institutions of the liberal world order that maintained it have crumbled. In the place of the patterns of trade, infrastructure and political order that once felt like inevitable parts of the postcolonial world, we are witnessing the reappearance of the older routes of exchange.

For instance, we see the re-emergence of the Trans-Saharan routes, the trading routes into East and Central Africa and East-West connections across the Sahel and the Red Sea. In South Africa, there are calls to dissolve the Union of South Africa, which in 1910 joined the British Cape Colony with the independent Boer republics of the Transvaal and Free State as well as Natal. Yemen has been redividing for over a decade now in ways that are reminiscent of the 19th century, and of course Russian aggression has called into question the stability of eastern Europe’s borders.

These are just a few examples of how the stability that defined the second half of the 20th century cannot be taken for granted. As we think of what models might best explain statecraft after the liberal order, it increasingly makes sense to look at the 19th-century map as an example of political competition and shifting boundaries.

stories.title: When The Present Eats The Future

stories.body:
The Achilles heel of consumer democracies.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

The Achilles heel of consumer democracies is that there is precious little constituency for the future in the present. All the feedback signals — in politics, culture and the market — are geared to short-term gratification. In each case, the incentives of the system deliver what the most influential demographic wants, and when they want it, which is now.

From fast fashion to electoral contests to quarterly earnings reports, the system is responsive to the pursuit of happiness defined by the near horizon.

The consequence of this, which Harvard sociologist Daniel Bell argued more than half a century ago in his book, “The Cultural Contradictions of Capitalism,” is that the present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society. The recent Noema essay by Simon Curtis and Ian Klaus titled “Americans Are Losing The Long Game” is excellent on this point.

While state-guided dirigiste policies that champion and support strategic industries deemed critical for the future are roundly frowned upon in market economies, the opposite rigidity of the short-term consumerist mentality is less appreciated as a critical failure of good governance. Yet, unless societies prepare for, subsidize and invest in the kind of future they want, they will never get there.

“The present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society.”

China’s Market-State Modality

Of all the major powers, post-Mao China stands out in taking control of its future without sacrificing the present. Over recent decades, it has both lifted hundreds of millions into general prosperity while, at the same time, swiftly conquering the key industries of a sustainable future, from green technology to artificial intelligence.

One has to admit that the Middle Kingdom’s mix of a long-term planning framework checked by robust market signals and bolstered by strategically deployed subsidies has worked. Indeed, it has worked too well: Its overproduction is spilling out and flooding world markets, threatening to displace domestic jobs and industry elsewhere.

China has not arrived at this point overnight. It has been a long time coming. In 1987, the ideology chief of the Communist Party politburo at the time, Hu Qili, told me in Beijing: “The market is not a feature unique to capitalism. Capitalism does not have the patent right over the market economy. What we are trying to create is a new and unprecedented modality where planning is combined with the commodity economy, where the state regulates the market, and the market guides the enterprises.”

The overall economy is steered by a one-party political system designed to reach consensus over long-term goals that have the decisive thrust to be carried out over many years without a break in continuity. Once set, the policy path is followed with relative discipline by a leadership and administration that, while not based on popular appeal to an electorate, is systemically accountable for realizing its set objectives.

When a key strategic goal is ordained by the Party, the state fosters a “whole dragon” approach in which start-up subsidies, sourcing, supply chains and production capacity are vertically aligned, making it one of the most powerful production ensembles in economic history.

Flaws Linked To Strength

The chief flaw of China’s system, of course, is closely linked to its strength. To keep the consensus from fraying, it overcompensates on the side of repressive order and control of freedom. It is the opposite of the open societies of the West, where the flaw lies within the strength of diverse participation and electoral competition: a growing inability to forge a consensus on long-term goals out of the cacophony of voices, the welter of contending interests and the immediate wash of fickle public opinion.

When all-out competitive partisanship destroys consensus among the body politic, the democratic transfer of power can mean a complete rupture of policies endorsed by most voters only four years earlier. Sticking to the course for the time it takes to reach fruition is not a reliable feature of this system.

The extreme edge of this stark difference can be seen in the contrasting behavior of the current leadership in the U.S. and China. America’s leader relishes dominating the memes of the moment, battling his way through every 24-hour news cycle by firing off social media barrages at sundry foes. China’s near-dictatorial leader has used his amassed clout to chart out a roadmap for the next half century.

China’s Long March To Owning Green Technologies

Meeting in Mexico in 2012, the G-20 decided for the first time to put climate change on the agenda. In those days, the Berggruen Institute’s 21 st Century Council, a group of former heads of state and government, tech leaders and Nobel laureates, would meet with the chair of the G-20 each year to advise on its agenda. Read Noema in print.

That year’s chair, then Mexican president Felipe Calderón, invited the council for lunch in the garden of Los Pinos, the presidential palace, to discuss the upcoming meeting. When the topic turned to climate, Wu Jianmin, a top Chinese diplomat and executive director of the China Institute for Innovation and Development Strategy, related that a top priority of the then incoming Party leadership of Xi Jinping would be “ecological civilization.”

All those 14 years ago, he confidently laid out a trajectory of China’s decisive shift to electric vehicles and plans for massive R&D investment in battery storage for wind and solar as well as EVs. Everyone listened respectfully, but doubtfully, because China was then not even in the auto race.

In 2012, China already dominated solar panels, but the Chevy Volt was the world’s most produced EV. No nation commanded battery production, which then was only nascently entering global competition.

Wu’s confidence in China’s capacity to deliver was well-founded. Today, nearly 70% of all new car sales in China are EVs, and half of all sales globally are Chinese-made electric vehicles. China produces around 80% of the world’s batteries and holds 70% of global battery patents. Its hosts half of the entire world’s large-scale battery storage capacity, primarily to store solar and wind power for the grid when the sun isn’t shining or the wind blowing.

As part of its whole-dragon approach, China also built out the widely distributed infrastructure of rapid charging stations across the country necessary to boost EV use. It launched a strategic push to link battery storage to the grid, requiring developers to build or commission large-scale storage capacity as a condition for approval of new wind or solar installations.

China’s export of its technology has enabled the advance of large-scale batteries for integration into power grids in many countries. Some 70% of EV batteries worldwide are from China.

California has the most installed large battery storage facilities outside of China. Its capacity has grown from a mere 700 megawatts in 2019 to 21,000 MW in 2026. By 2045, the state aims to reach 52,000 MW capacity to support a 100% clean energy grid. For the entire month of May 2026, 51% of California’s total energy demand came from solar power. Blackouts during the intense heatwaves of recent years have been avoided because the grid was linked to off-hour battery storage from renewable energy.

Though often assembled in California, 90% of the cells and core components of the large-scale batteries the state has installed come from China.

Quotas And Dumping

From the standpoint of the race against time on climate, the widest possible dispersion of China’s green technology is a net plus for the planet. Yet, as in other realms of trade competition, its cheaper product and overproduction portends a vulnerable dependence on a political system which the West considers a strategic adversary.

To the extent domestic industries exist, China’s prowess threatens to run them out of business. Since green technology is critical to our future, the most sensible approach would not be to prohibit Chinese imports, but set a reasonable quota beyond which tariffs would kick in. That would both limit the damage while allowing competition from abroad to spark the scale-up of domestic industry.

Free-market ideologues aside, subsidies are not the end of the world when a livable biosphere is at stake. After all, up until the Trump administration, the U.S. did manage for a time to escape the pull of consumer immediacy. For years, it subsidized the purchase of EVs with tax rebates. And California has shown how regulation creates, not destroys, markets. Elon Musk’s Tesla empire would never have emerged if it were not for the state’s fuel efficiency and clean energy standards, which created the market for his technology.

“Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China?”

Is It Impolitic To Learn From China?

Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China? This is not, of course, to imply in any way that the West turn toward autocracy or authoritarianism. It is only to warn that unless democracies can look beyond the short-term horizon and find ways to reach a governing consensus that sticks, they will be left in the dust of the oncoming future.

To turn an old Chinese saying toward ourselves: “The stones from hills yonder can polish jade at home.”

The councils' leaders say services will be hit due to funding cuts

Published 4 hours ago

Four London council leaders have formally submitted a challenge to government reforms that are set to see their central funding slashed by up to 58%.

The leaders of Wandsworth, Richmond, Westminster and Kensington and Chelsea councils delivered revised funding proposals to the Treasury on Thursday urging the government to rethink its overhaul of local authority funding rules.

Among those councils, the leaders said the reforms would result in funding cuts ranging from 40% to 58% by 2029.

The government said the "outdated" local authority funding model was being reformed to ensure "money goes where it is most needed".

'Every route available'

The changes, known as the Fair Funding Review 2.0, aim to shift more cash towards areas with higher deprivation.

Wandsworth's Conservative administration said the reforms would cut funding by 40% and force it to slash services and raise council tax.

The authority is proposing to raise council tax by 94% from April, in addition to making sweeping cuts – including shutting its cost-of-living reserve with £6.2m of unspent funds, replacing Labour's Access for All with a much smaller concessionary scheme, cancelling its Borough of Sanctuary status and suspending voluntary sector grants for four years.

Kensington and Chelsea is set to lose £108m, or more than 40% of its central funding over the next four years under the reforms, while Westminster is due to see these resources drop by around £100m (46%). Richmond is set to be stripped of £26m (58%) of its core funding.

The councils have now formally submitted their revised funding proposals, under the Sustainable Communities Act, asking the government to reconsider its decision.

Wandsworth Council leader Robert Morritt, who heads a Conservative minority administration, said: "Residents should not have to pick up the bill for changes imposed by Whitehall. This proposal takes our case directly to government.

"We are using every route available to fight for a fairer deal and protect Wandsworth taxpayers."

stories.summary: Martin Griffiths, Reform-UK Leader of North Northants Council, says: "We have nothing to hide."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The steelworks in Corby, pictured, closed in 1981

Published 22 October 2026, 13:01 BST

A council leader says he will support a public inquiry into contaminated land in a town, following a report published last week that revealed it could pose a risk to human health.

The charity Earthwatch Europe says trained citizen scientists have found potentially harmful levels of metal or metalloid at 52 freshwater sites across Corby.

Children in Corby have been born with birth defects, believed to have been caused when steelworks were demolished in the 1980s.

As first reported in the NN Journal, Martin Griffiths, Reform-UK Leader of North Northamptonshire Council said: "We have nothing to hide."

He added: "We would welcome a genuinely independent examination of the historic events and the questions that remain unanswered, and we would cooperate fully with any inquiry established by the government."

Griffiths challenged the Labour MP for Corby and East Northamptonshire, Lee Barron, to take his longstanding calls for a public inquiry directly to the Labour government.

"If Lee Barron and his Government believe a public inquiry is necessary, we are ready to support his efforts to secure one," added Griffiths.

In response, Lee Barron said it was "baffling" the council would ask for a public inquiry.

He said the authority needed to immediately publish a plan to investigate and clean up any contaminated land.

Barron said: "It is important that North Northamptonshire Council investigate the [Earthwatch] report.

"People deserve answers and it is the role of the council to provide them."

Earthwatch Europe said volunteers found the chemical element cadmium in six freshwater samples in July

Earlier this week, Barron wrote to both the leader of North Northamptonshire Council and the Health Secretary Yvette Cooper.

In his letters, seen by the BBC, he said the findings from the environmental charity "need to be investigated as a matter of urgency".

He has also called on the health secretary to "ensure North Northamptonshire Council take immediate action to clean up any contaminated land".

Parents are calling for more transparency around issues they believe are causing illnesses

Earlier this year, a number of families gathered outside North Northamptonshire's Corby headquarters calling for a public inquiry to clarify the situation.

Des Collins, the solicitor who represented families affected by the town's toxic waste scandal, said: "We welcome the leader's announcement, which finally admits what we have been telling his council for the past year - our clients need, and deserve, a public inquiry as it is the only feasible way of getting to the truth behind the disposal of toxic waste around Corby.

"We look forward to Lee Barron MP and North Northamptonshire Council working together to encourage the Cabinet Office to authorise the Inquiry without further delay.

"Quite literally, local lives depend on it."

The government has been approached for comment.

stories.title: Police should not be scared to wade in to stop wrongdoing, says Badenoch
stories.summary: The Tory leader calls for more support for police officers and the public when they step in to help.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch speaking at the Police Federation conference in London

Published 5 hours ago

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised punishments for people who intervene to "do the right thing" in a speech at the Police Federation conference.

Telling delegates she was "not scared to wade in", she called for more support for members of the public as well as police officers who step in to stop wrongdoing.

Badenoch also criticised Labour for failing to send a minister to the conference for two years in a row.

The prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman rejected the claims, stating the police have the government's "full backing" and are benefitting from investment. The BBC has contacted the Home Office for comment on ministerial attendance at the police conference.

In a speech at the conference, Badenoch said: "Too often these days, we fail to recognise sacrifice and service.

"Whether it's hounding brave and elderly veterans through the courts, hounding police officers who try to do the right thing, or even ordinary members of the public who step in to help only to find that they're in trouble themselves.

"It's no wonder the people in this country are becoming too scared to wade in, too scared to do the right thing. Well, I am different. I am not scared to wade in, and I am not scared to back the police."

The Conservative leader listed police officers who have been killed in the line of duty, such as PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough who died in the Cleveland A66 crash, and PC Andrew Harper , killed investigating a quad bike theft.

She also attacked police being investigated following controversial cases, including the case of 24-year-old Chris Kaba , who was shot by Sgt Matthew Blake in 2022 after he tried to ram his way past police cars.

The police officer was put on trial for murder before being cleared, with Badenoch saying his "job was made harder because he didn't get the backing he deserved".

Badenoch also attacked Labour, saying: "I think it is telling that for two years in a row, the Labour Government has not sent anyone to address this conference – not the policing minister, not the Home Secretary.

"You are the ones who enforce the law. You are the ones who ensure there are consequences for bad behaviour. That's why, if we want law and order back in our country, back on our streets, we need to back the police."

Responding, the prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman said: "I would reject those claims.

"The police have the government's full backing and as you will have seen from various reports this morning, we are continuing to invest in our police and we are bringing forward reforms following the Bernard Hogan Howe report in due course."

The Home Office has been contacted for comment about ministerial attendance at the conference and whether the government is still planning to recruit 13,000 police officers.

stories.title: Ten councillors quit after leader's fraud conviction
stories.summary: Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of defrauding the county council out of thousands of pounds.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion

Published 22 October 2026, 12:25 BST

Ten Ashfield Independent councillors have quit the party this week following the former leader's fraud conviction.

Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion last month

He resigned as leader of Ashfield District Council the following day, but was later given a seat on the authority's planning committee .

As of Thursday, 13 councillors are sitting as non-aligned independents, while 18 Ashfield Independents remain, meaning the party is one councillor away from losing its majority.

Zadrozny was accused of setting up a fake heritage group to defraud Nottinghamshire County Council out of thousands of pounds.

Prosecutors also alleged that he had failed to pay tax on four rental properties.

The 46-year-old, who served as an Ashfield Independents councillor on the county council, was told by the judge he would be sentenced on 27 November, and was "at risk of an immediate custodial sentence".

The Ashfield Independents now have a majority of one

Councillors Warren Nuttall and Kier Barsby had quit the Ashfield Independents group prior to this week.

One of the 10 members to quit this week is John Wilmott, a cabinet member who is also a Nottinghamshire county councillor for Hucknall North.

Another is the chairman of the council, Dale Grounds.

Councillor Matt Relf, executive lead member for growth, regeneration and local planning, said quitting the party was an "enormously upsetting" decision.

"The understandable controversy around Jason's conviction and the choices he made that led to that have upset and surprised a lot of people in the group," he said.

"With the election of a new leader we hoped that would put everything behind us, but unfortunately the decision to appoint Jason back on to the planning committee was just a step too far.

"That decision was made with no consultation with the broader group.

"To stay true to our principles of integrity and democratic accountability I was left with no option but to leave, and I think others have reached the same conclusion."

Hucknall Central councillor Lee Waters, who was another one of the councillors to quit this week, said his decision "follows a period of reflection, and I believe the time is right to move on".

"Throughout my time as a councillor, my priority has been to listen to residents, address their concerns and work hard on the issues that matter to our community. That remains unchanged," he added.

"I will continue carrying out my council responsibilities and dealing with ongoing casework with the same commitment and dedication as always."

Lee Anderson, the MP for Ashfield, posted on Facebook to warn that former Ashfield Independent councillors would not be accepted into Reform UK.

He said there would be "no deals" between the parties.

Samantha Deakin has taken over as leader of the council, but has so far declined the BBC's request for an interview.

Fiona Fillingham attended the demonstration on Thursday

A demonstration was held outside the council house on Thursday in protest at Zadrozny being able to remain as a council.

Protesters told the BBC they had been "let down" by the authority.

John Green, of the Ashfield Community Action Group, said: "We are disgusted that the Ashfield Independents have voted a convicted fraudster onto the planning a committee."

Tim Curtis, who also attended the demonstration, said: "There's no mechanism to get him out. He should stand down from the council and not be anywhere near making any decisions."

Fiona Fillingham, a local business owner, added: "If I got done for fraud I am sure I wouldn't get my job back.

"It seems backhanded, shoddy, unfair and unrealistic. They can't keep getting away with it."

stories.title: Tank barrel production returns to UK after 20 years
stories.summary: The defence secretary says the UK is "back in the business of making weapons" for its armed forces.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Rheinmetall said the facility had created 100 jobs and it would look to expand its workforce in the future

Published 22 October 2026, 13:14 BST

The production of gun barrels to be used on tanks has returned to the UK for the first time in 20 years with the opening of a new manufacturing facility.

The UK Gun Hall in Telford, run by German defence firm Rheinmetall, has supported 100 jobs and will make barrels and breaches for large calibre weapons.

Defence secretary, Wes Streeting, attended the opening ceremony on Thursday and said Britain was "back in the business of making weapons" for its armed forces.

"From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action," he said.

"One hundred skilled jobs in world class manufacturing and the return of large calibre weapon production to UK soil for the first time in 20 years - this is what defence as an engine for growth looks like," Streeting added.

The barrels and breaches will be made for both 120m and 155mm weapon systems, including for the RCH 155 and future artillery platforms, according to Rheinmetall.

The firm is already involved in the UK's Boxer combat vehicle programme and is upgrading the country's Challenger tanks .

Wes Streeting said the opening of the facility would be a boost to Britain's defence capabilities

Specialist workers from Telford have been recruited and the firm said it would expand its workforce as production ramped up.

Ahead of the factory's opening, staff spent time at a Rheinmetall facility in Germany where they were trained in precision manufacturing, quality assurance and specialist weapon production.

Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall, said the gun hall was an "important milestone" that would strengthen the country's industrial base "for decades to come".

"We are committed to investing in the UK for the long term, expanding our industrial footprint and working together to deliver the capabilities needed for the future," he added.

'Statement of intent'

Papperger told BBC Radio Shropshire it was a significant investment in Telford, adding that the firm only had one similar production line in Germany.

"At the moment, we have a lot of orders and we need the capacity. Telford has very well-educated people, highly-motivated people," he added.

Papperger said the company currently had 1,300 employees in the UK but was looking to build up that number.

During his speech at the event, Streeting described Telford as being "synonymous with engineering and manufacturing".

"Today is a vote of confidence in our country," he continued, "a statement of intent on our mission to reindustrialise Britain and create good, well-paid jobs across our country."

stories.title: Who is Chancellor John Healey? Labour veteran who quit as defence secretary
stories.summary: The softly-spoken former defence secretary is gearing up for the biggest moment of his long political career.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 July 2026

Andy Burnham's decision to appoint John Healey to the crucial role of chancellor of the exchequer was the rarest of things at Westminster - a genuine surprise.

It's not that the 66-year-old lacked experience or credibility - just that he had not been seen as a likely contender, with all the speculation about who would replace Rachel Reeves centring on more high-profile figures.

Healey had flown under the radar since his explosive resignation as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June this year.

His assessment of the government's defence investment plan - that it fell "well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time" - was devastating and undoubtedly hastened Sir Keir's departure from Downing Street.

But his resignation letter also included pointed criticism of Reeves's Treasury, which he said had been "unwilling" to "commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats".

Now he is in the Treasury hot seat and under pressure to spell out how he will get defence spending up to 3% of national income, at the same time as cutting government borrowing costs and tackling the cost of living.

Like his predecessor, he faces the difficult balancing act of keeping Labour MPs happy without spooking the financial markets, while delivering on the government's key priorities.

Never the flashiest of politicians, his early speeches as chancellor have been focused on stressing his commitment to fiscal discipline and cutting the welfare bill, as well as banging the drum for Burnham's plan to "reindustrialise" Britain.

But he did show his lighter side in a social media video with the prime minister, which saw "Andy and John" bantering about twiglets and scampi fries in the pub. , external

"I will always stand by my political choices as chancellor, including pork scratchings as the best pub snack," he revealed on X.

John Healey: The Basics

Age: 66

Place of birth: Wakefield, West Yorkshire

Education: Lady Lumley's Academy, Pickering; St Peter's School, York; Christ's College, Cambridge

Family: He married Jackie Bate in 1993. The couple have one son, Alex

Constituency: MP for Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, in South Yorkshire

Salary: £166,000

What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 2 days ago

Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor Published 28 September

The softly-spoken Yorkshireman has a remarkable record as someone who has been on the Labour frontbench almost continuously since 2001.

Born in Wakefield in 1960 and educated at Lady Lumley's Comprehensive School, Pickering, and Peter's School in York, he studied social and political science at Christ's College, Cambridge.

Before entering politics, he worked as a journalist, briefly editing Parliament's in-house magazine The House, before becoming a disability rights campaigner and trade union official.

He is married and has one son.

He first came into Parliament in Tony Blair's landslide general election in 1997 as MP for Wentworth, a former mining area north of Sheffield, which following boundary changes is now Rawmarsh and Conisbrough.

He retained the seat with a majority of 6,908 in the 2024 general election, with a Reform UK candidate in second place.

In the early 2000s, he held a string of ministerial posts, including housing, local government in the Blair and Gordon Brown governments.

He spent five years at Brown's Treasury where he oversaw policies such as the child trust funds and attempts to regenerate and devolve power - the Regional Development Agencies, later scrapped by the coalition government.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson , Healey said: "The Treasury's a paradox. You have some of the very best and brightest officials in the Treasury, but you have too often a Treasury orthodox that's a dead hand on dynamic government."

He added that maintaining financial stability was a key function of the Treasury but "also it can and it has to drive economic growth, raise levels of productivity, support business competition, investment for the for the future".

And he claimed the department "was in denial about the commitment that the UK has rightly made to NATO and to our people" to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, which would not come until 2034/35 under current plans.

"The Treasury still often sees defence as a drain on public spending and not the driver of economic growth that we've demonstrated in two years," he told Nick Robinson.

Healey's other area of expertise is housing. He served as shadow housing secretary when Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader, despite supporting a failed attempt to oust Corbyn in 2016.

Pundits had not touted Healey (right, dressed in a suit) as a frontrunner for the chancellor job

When Sir Keir was elected Labour leader in 2020, he made Healey shadow defence secretary, becoming defence secretary when Labour came to power four years later.

Healey was a staunch supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and made several trips to the country to meet President Zelensky.

At his first meeting with Nato allies, in September 2024, he said he was "confident" Labour could honour a commitment to increase defence spending and "make the decisions that allow us to set out a long-term plan to make our forces better equipped to fight and to deter the threats we face".

Healey also drove investment in housing for armed forces families , with a £9bn spending plan.

Despite his low key style, he proved capable of delivering stern warnings to the UK's enemies.

In April this year, he delivered a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin , in a briefing on "covert" operations by Russian sumbmarines, saying: "We see you.

"We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences."

Following the announcement of the defence investment plan, he condemned what he called "Treasury trickery" and the lack of clarity on what new money the Ministry of Defence would get.

Healey also made clear that he wanted a clear plan to increase UK defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.

He is not expected to do that in his first Budget, with key spending decisions set to be unveiled next year.

But the tax and spending decisions he does announce on 28 October will still have a huge impact on the success or failure of the fledgling Burnham administration.

stories.title: Tougher punishments for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing backed by victim's family
stories.summary: The aunt of Zara Aleena says the new powers for judges will "rebalance the power" from offender to victim.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Zara Aleena, a 35-year-old law graduate, was sexually assaulted and murdered by Jordan McSweeney in June 2022

Published 22 October 2026, 02:17 BST

Tougher punishments for offenders who refuse to attend their sentencings will "rebalance the power" in the justice system, the aunt of murder victim Zara Aleena has said.

From next year, prisoners could be blocked from prison visits and confined to their cells for weeks on end if they do not follow orders to go to court.

This builds on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years.

"A year or two added to a life sentence wouldn't make any difference to an offender. But taking away these privileges would," Farah Naz said.

Naz said the refusal of the man who murdered her niece to go to his sentencing "left a sense that justice was not quite complete".

Aleena, an aspiring lawyer, was murdered by Jordan McSweeney as she walked home from an east London bar in June 2022.

McSweeney remained in his cell when he was sentenced to life in prison at the Old Bailey later that year.

He was jailed for at least 38 years, which was later reduced to 33 years after he won a Court of Appeal challenge .

Naz said Zara's Aleena's family had hoped that by reading their victim impact statement in front of her murderer, he would see "the consequence of his actions, of what he'd done, the devastation that he had caused".

She added that the new measures would "bring accountability and rebalance the power in the justice system from offender to victim."

Offenders who refuse to attend sentencing can already face a fine or up to two years additional imprisonment for contempt of court.

But the Ministry of Justice has acknowledged that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter those already behind bars.

The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, while social visits could be banned for 27 days and other prison privileges revoked for longer.

Judges will also be able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for a period of almost three months.

For criminals aged 18-20, similar restrictions could be handed down, but for shorter periods of time, the Ministry of Justice said.

However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions.

"Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said.

"Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences," she added.

But Pia Sinha, the CEO of Prison Reform Trust, has called for evidence that sanctions will increase attendance and warned the measures will punish relatives of prisoners who "have committed no offence themselves".

The families of murdered primary school teacher Sabina Nessa and mother-of-three Jan Mustafa joined Zara Aleena's family in campaigning for changes to the laws.

All of their loved ones' killers did not attend their sentencing hearings.

Thomas Cashman, the gunman who murdered nine-year-old Olivia Pratt-Korbel, and triple crossbow and knife killer Kyle Clifford, also refused to face their punishment in court.

Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, said the announcement followed "tireless efforts of victims' families" not accepting offenders simply "opting out of facing justice".

She said it was "essential" the powers were used "consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve".

stories.title: MI5 spied on NHS founder Nye Bevan for more than 20 years, newly released files show
stories.summary: He came to Security Service's attention in the 1930s when he was considered a left-wing firebrand.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Papers show Aneurin Bevan first came to the attention of the security service in the 1930s

Published 22 October 2026, 10:35 BST

NHS founder Aneurin "Nye" Bevan was spied on by MI5 for more than 20 years, according to newly released files.

Papers given to the National Archives show he first came to the attention of the Security Service in the 1930s when he was considered a firebrand left-winger linked to prominent communists.

Monitoring continued after Bevan, from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, became a minister in the post-war Labour government when he drove through the creation of the NHS in the face of opposition from doctors.

At one stage the-then MI5 director general became so concerned about his links to a Russian spy that he went to see Prime Minister Clement Attlee in No 10 to warn him.

But some in the service questioned why it was taking an interest in him, given everything he did was in the open.

After his death in 1960, one MI5 officer called the content of the file "remarkably tame".

The papers show MI5 first opened a file on Bevan when he was backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in 1933.

One of the first reports included an account of an anti-Nazi rally in Montreal, Canada, which Bevan addressed in 1934.

"Bevan has inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the Communist cause," it said.

In 1943, Roger Hollis, future director general, summarised what they knew of Bevan's activities.

In 1933 he said the MP had been "in close touch" with Communist Party of Great Britain general secretary Harry Pollitt and party members who backed his plan to organise "workers' freedom groups" to defend against "capitalists".

Although there was nothing in the files to indicate MI5 tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, some wondered why they were watching him at all.

One MI5 director general was so worried about Bevan's links to a Russian spy he went to see Prime Minister Clement Attlee (left) about it

"I do not think that Bevan's activities are a matter in which we, the security service, should be involved," one officer wrote in 1943.

"In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently."

The reporting continued after the war when Bevan was made health minister in Attlee's government.

In 1949 MI5 became increasingly concerned about Bevan's friendship with Wilfred Macartney, "an unsavoury, unscrupulous character" convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.

Recordings of conversations suggested he was passing information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt.

That May the Security Service's chief Sir Percy Sillitoe took evidence to Attlee, who dismissed Macartney's claims as a "tissue of lies" but agreed to warn Bevan about him.

One of the final reports dates from 1954 when Bevan, now back in opposition, was invited to meet the Soviet ambassador, Yakov Malik, at London's Polish embassy.

The event "went off very badly", partly because the Russian had difficulty in understanding Bevan's accent, which led to misunderstanding.

"The party broke up in a none too friendly atmosphere," the report said.

The file was not closed until 1975 - 15 years after Bevan died.

stories.summary: A report by MPs urges the UK to address capability gaps including a lack of Royal Navy warships and submarines, as Russia seeks to dominate the region.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A UK carrier conducts operations in the High North and Arctic

Published 22 October 2026, 03:09 BST

The UK has "glaring gaps" in its ability to defend the Arctic region, leaving it vulnerable to potential Russian attacks, a report by MPs has warned.

The Commons Defence Committee said a shortage of Royal Navy warships and submarines was leaving the country's critical infrastructure in the High North, including undersea cables and energy supplies, exposed.

In the event of a conflict, the report added that Russia could threaten the UK's population, civilian and military infrastructure and vital supply routes across the Atlantic from the US.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said it is "clear-eyed about the threat Russia posed" and is investing heavily to protect Britain's undersea cables.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer previously warned that Russia could attack Nato by the end of the decade.

The High North - which includes the Arctic circle and areas adjacent to it - has become central to the UK's defence concerns in recent years.

Earlier this year, the MoD said Russian submarine activity in the North Atlantic is now back to the same levels as the Cold War era.

In the new report, MPs highlighted a "shockingly low availability" of submarines and said there was a temporary loss in ability to operate them beneath Arctic ice.

"Russia can then use the ice to conceal and protect its own submarines while threatening Nato sea lanes, UK critical infrastructure and the UK's nuclear deterrent," it added.

Chair of the Defence Committee, Tan Dhesi, said: "This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage."

The work to address these gaps "cannot start soon enough," he added.

In light of uncertainty over US support for Nato, the report said the UK should consider whether the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force (Jef), a UK-led military coalition of northern European nations, should focus more on the High North.

An MoD spokesperson said the Jef was already "strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats".

Conservative shadow minister for war readiness Stuart Anderson said: "If Nato could be at war with Russia as soon as 2030, as the former prime minister warned, that means time is just as important as money.

"To deter war we must be ready for it, that means spending money now, not kicking the can down the road until it's too late".

stories.title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
stories.summary: For the first time, the Treasury calculates how much the UK could have raised by investing North Sea proceeds.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig in the North Sea.

Published 22 October 2026, 00:27 BST

After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.

Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding housed in the National Wealth Fund.

A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks.

It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go?

It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time.

"The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said.

"If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds."

On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth.

The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's.

"Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me.

It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said.

Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Published 1 day ago

It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era.

The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories.

Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996.

The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s.

I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund.

Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic.

It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future.

While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance.

UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits.

Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that.

Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is, what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past?

stories.title: Angry scenes and protests at Senedd as Reform call for ban on Muslim face coverings
stories.summary: Members of Reform called for Muslim religious face coverings, such as the burka, to be banned.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
After the debate a number of Plaid Cymru and Labour politicians took part in a protest on the Senedd steps - with Safa Elhassan addressing those gathered

Published 21 October 2026

There were bad-tempered and dramatic exchanges in the Senedd on Wednesday night as members of Reform called for Muslim religious face coverings, such as the burka, to be banned.

Politicians from the party said they were "anti-British", allowed Muslim women to hide their identities and suggested they represented an "alien culture".

Plaid Cymru and Labour politicians responded with disdain - Deputy First Minister Sioned Williams raised the Nuremberg Laws of 1930s Germany and how they led to the extermination of Jews.

The Muslim Council of Wales described "disturbingly authoritarian attitudes" - Reform's Jason O'Connell accused the group of trying to "silence" the debate.

There was no vote on the topic. The Senedd would have no power to ban face coverings.

A protest, including some Members of the Senedd (MSs), took place on the Senedd steps.

It is the latest heated debate in the Senedd on a Wednesday prompted by Reform MSs - previous include a discussion about the Nation of Sanctuary and calls for foreign nationals to be banned from house shares .

A niqab is a form of a veil used by Muslim women

Reform UK has previously said it would ban face coverings in public places , including burkas and balaclavas, if it won power at the next Westminster election.

Opening the debate to a nearly full chamber, Reform UK MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, Jason O'Connell, began by speaking about young men wearing balaclavas.

"From Newport to Rhyl, balaclava-clad young men, often dangerously riding illegal e-bikes, have been fuelling anti-social behaviour and making our streets feel unsafe," he said.

"For these individuals, face coverings are a way to conceal their identity, to make it harder for authorities to hold them accountable.

"And while governments across the UK turn a blind eye to this, Reform says enough is enough now, face coverings have no place in British and Welsh society."

Turning to the burka, O'Connell, who called Wednesday's debate, said: "We have no issue or problem with Islam or Muslims."

With opposing members heckling as he spoke, he added: "We do have an issue with people living amongst our communities hiding their identities.

"We say the same thing to protesters that cover their face, whatever their political persuasion."

Jason O'Connell called the short debate on face coverings late on Wednesday night

Amid frequent interruptions, fellow Reform MS Francesca O'Brien told the Senedd that face coverings, including the burka, were "anti-British".

"Not all cultures are equal," she said. "We cannot continue to import alien cultures into this country and expect integration.

"Oppressive beliefs are totally at odds with our history and culture.

"Banning these coverings is simple, common sense."

Reform MS Joe Martin said the burka and niqab were "two of the many ways in which fundamentalist Islam is uniquely incompatible with Western civilization".

"We can't even see the faces of thousands of people who've moved here. If two Muslim women live in the same street and they both wear burkas, how are we meant to tell them apart?

"Assimilation means losing religious face coverings and to encourage that they should be banned."

The burka is a veil worn by some Muslim women that covers the face and body, often leaving a mesh screen to see through.

It covers more of the face than a niqab, a veil that leaves the area around the eyes clear.

In comparison, a hijab is a headscarf that in the West most commonly covers the head and neck but leaves the face clear.

A protest took place on the steps of the Senedd before the debate on Wednesday

Williams said the debate was a "shameful" end to a "sad day" that began with the commemoration of the Aberfan disaster .

Looking at the Reform members, she accused them of "conflating the intimidating behaviour of thugs and those whose protest can descend into disorder and violence, often in demonstrations directed against migrants or Muslims, with the very people who are targeted by that intimidating behaviour".

"I do not accept that a face covering worn by an individual for religious reasons means they don't share British or Welsh values," she said.

"Nor should we suggest that someone belongs any less, because their religious practice differs from that of others."

Williams added: "The Jewish people of 1930s Germany were subject to the Nuremberg Laws, which stated they were no longer German, laws which led to their persecution and extermination by the state that stripped them of the Germaness.

"Who decides that a woman who [has] a face covering is less British or less Welsh?"

The comments led to angry protests and finger pointing from the Reform benches.

A point of order was raised by a member of the party asking the presiding officer if the comments were appropriate.

The presiding officer Huw Irranca-Davies said he was "always happy" to review the record of proceedings, but did not make a ruling.

Williams said she was making a "statement of fact".

Carrie Harper, Plaid MS for Fflint Wrecsam, told Reform UK: "How on earth can you claim to stand up for women when you are trying to dictate what Muslim women can and cannot wear?"

Plaid MS Kiera Marshall, for Caerdydd Penarth, said a Muslim woman in her constituency was subject to a "physical, violent attack in broad daylight".

"The attacker shouted at her about removing her headscarf and continued to do exactly this while physically assaulting her," she said.

"This is just one example of an increasingly common occurrence when Muslim women are being targeted.

"This is exactly what the rhetoric that Reform is peddling is doing."

Labour's Huw Thomas said he had not heard Reform condemn "the masked mobs who stormed RNLI stations across of South Coast, last month".

A lifeboat station in Portsmouth went out of service in September, following anti-migrant protests.

Following the debate, Dr Abdul Azim Ahmed of the Muslim Council of Wales said: "This debate demonstrated the disturbingly authoritarian attitudes members of Reform UK hold, coupled with dangerously ultra nationalist attitudes about culture and belonging."

Suwayba Hussein accused Reform of using the debate "to push Islamophobia"

Ahead of the debate, a protest took place on the Senedd steps, with Plaid Cymru and Labour MSs later joining them.

One of those taking part, Suwayba Hussein from Cardiff, accused Reform of using the debate "to push Islamophobia".

"We're trying to just live our lives, we integrate really well, and this is just going to increase the Islamophobia that we see in modern-day society," she said.

"The Reform party are a racist party, and this is another way of them pushing their racism into mainstream debate."

During the debate, O'Connell said that accusations of racism and Islamophobia against Reform were "tired, ineffective, and clearly wildly inaccurate".

Opposition politicians and parties are able to use the Senedd on a Wednesday to raise issues that they want discussed, and individual members can trigger so-called "short debates".

Since the election, Reform - which is the second largest group in the Welsh Parliament - has used Wednesdays to raise topics that have resulted in angry debates.

The topic of short debates must not contain language considered by the presiding officer to be disorderly, discriminatory or offensive.

BBC Wales was told before the debate proceeded that the Senedd's presiding officer, Irranca-Davies, did not consider the title - "full-face coverings are against British values" - to be against the guidance.
