stories.title: US official: Russia's stalker satellite sure looks like an orbital weapon
stories.summary: The Russian official who called commercial satellites "legitimate targets" now says concerns are "unfounded."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Russian official who called commercial satellites “legitimate targets” now says concerns are “unfounded.”

Four years ago, a senior official in Russia’s foreign ministry painted a bullseye on commercial satellite networks that assist Ukraine in its fight against invading Russian military forces.

On Wednesday, several days after a Russian military spacecraft moved within striking distance of one of those commercial satellites, the same Russian diplomat assured the world there’s no reason to worry.

There’s a sharp incongruity in those statements from Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of Russia’s delegation to the United Nations. Vorontsov’s comments Wednesday in the UN General Assembly’s First Committee came moments after a US official called attention to recent maneuvers by Kosmos 2612 , a Russian military craft that approached a US-registered commercial satellite some 340 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth.

“Just last weekend, Russia’s Ministry of Defense Kosmos 2612 exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite,” Brian Hardesty, a US State Department official, told the UN committee. “These behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation. The decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless and violated long-established safety thresholds in low-Earth orbit.”

Thomas DiNanno, the US Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security, shared a similar statement on X . The comments were the first from the US government since the close encounter last weekend.

Vorontsov said the US government’s concerns, echoed by European officials, were “unfounded” distractions. “Western countries headed by the United States continue to use loudspeaker diplomacy repeating absurd accusations about Russia’s space activity.”

All Russian activity in space is “purely peaceful in character,” Vorontsov said. “This applies to the activity related to Kosmos 2612.”

There’s a history

Vorontsov’s statements in 2022 were more provocative. At that time, as Ukraine ramped up its reliance on commercial satellite communications and surveillance, Vorontsov said that commercial space infrastructure used by Ukraine’s military, including Western satellites, could be a “legitimate target for a retaliatory strike.”

It is no wonder, then, that the Russian military’s unprecedented maneuvers near one of those satellites raised alarms. Since its launch in April, Kosmos 2612 performed a series of carefully choreographed rocket burns to match orbits with ICEYE-X36, a radar surveillance satellite owned by the US subsidiary of the Finnish remote sensing company ICEYE.

These maneuvers follow several Russian tests in recent years of suspected anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons, including a system called Nivelir, which can fire a projectile at high speed to smash into another object in orbit. Russia’s co-orbital ASAT experiments date back to the Soviet era.

“Countries can, of course, deny until they are blue in the face that they have weapons in orbit, but observable and confirmable behaviors are hard to deny,” said Jessup Taylor, the US Deputy Permanent Representative to the Conference on Disarmament. “What you do up there speaks much louder than what you say down here.”

Last week, Kosmos 2612 moved closer and held position in “extreme proximity” to ICEYE-X36, according to orbital intelligence company LeoLabs. An executive at LeoLabs told Ars on Monday that Kosmos 2612 moved within 500 meters (about 1,640 feet) of the ICEYE satellite, and likely much closer. An image from Vantor, a satellite remote-sensing company, first published by Axios , showed the satellites about 1 kilometer apart on Saturday.

Taylor suggested Wednesday that Kosmos 2612 may have ultimately closed within a range of 100 feet. It’s hard to know for sure due to the limitations of satellite tracking.

“I would note that Russia did not attempt to explain why a Russian military satellite moved within tens of meters of another country’s commercial satellite,” Taylor said. “The decision to conduct operations violated long-established safety thresholds in low-Earth orbit.”

Kosmos 2612 backed off from ICEYE-X36 without firing a shot and is orbiting far away, although its trajectory does not preclude attempting another approach.

In September, Pentagon officials acknowledged for the first time that the US military possesses space-based weapons. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink announced the news, but he did not reveal any information about the weapons. The United States, Russia, China, and India previously tested ground-launched anti-satellite missiles, but the US government is the first to admit the placement of weapons in orbit.

Examples of China’s weapons testing in space include a 2021 demonstration of a Fractional Orbital Bombardment System , and demos of robotic arms and highly maneuverable satellites that could be used for servicing and repair or the inspection and capture of an adversary’s spacecraft.

Much of the discussion at the UN on Wednesday focused on proposals by Russia and China for an international agreement to ban the placement of any weapons in space. US officials say such proposals are moot because the world’s leading space powers already possess them. There’s also the thorny question of how to determine what constitutes a weapon in space, where ramming and jamming could be done by conventional technologies flying on many kinds of satellites.

Such blanket bans are “ineffectual and unrealistic,” Hardesty said. They would “ inevitably be violated by its proponents while interfering with our ability to defend against those who would cheat on their obligations.”

Instead, US officials have underscored a tenet of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit. In 2024, under the Biden administration, the United States proposed a resolution in the UN Security Council that would have reaffirmed the ban, two months after a US intelligence leak suggested Russia was developing a nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon. Russia vetoed the UN resolution .

All of this is happening amid a slowdown in SpaceX’s Starlink or Starshield broadband service in Ukraine, affecting the country’s use of satellite connectivity to support drone operations. The decision to restrict Starlink service in Ukraine, whether directed by SpaceX or the US government , came after President Trump and Elon Musk criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries.

Satellites like the ICEYE platform, meanwhile, provide overhead imaging to support Ukraine’s efforts to target Russian battlefield forces and strike deeper into Russian territory.

stories.title: Electric or gas? BMW goes both ways with new 2027 X5 and iX5.
stories.summary: 460 kW charging and 450 miles of range are among the reasons the EV is the one to get.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
460 kW charging and 450 miles of range are among the reasons the EV is the one to get.

When we first drove BMW’s first Neue Klasse model, the iX3 , it quickly revealed that BMW knows how to make a good electric vehicle. A clean-sheet design, it featured the automaker’s sixth-generation electric powertrain , a completely reimagined dashboard, and powerful computers to run the whole show. Now, much of that technology is being ported over to the larger X5 line.

But BMW knows not all its customers are ready to go electric, especially in the US, so it’s sticking with its powertrain-agnostic CLAR platform, as used in cars as diverse as the large 7 Series and the new gasoline 3 Series. Which means in addition to the all-electric iX5, there are also mild hybrid and plug-in hybrid X5s available, and in time, even a hydrogen-powered option. For now, as I’ll explain, I think the EV is the pick of the bunch.

Pick your power

The most conventional option is the X5 40 xDrive, powered by a 3.0 L turbocharged inline six-cylinder engine that generates 394 hp (294 kW) and 428 lb-ft (580 Nm). The 48 V mild hybrid system can contribute a decent slug of torque (148 lb-ft/200 Nm) if necessary, and the engine operates under the Miller cycle for better efficiency, as well as featuring the usual BMW engine technology, like variable valve timing. Expect around 26 mpg (9 L/100 km) from this powertrain and a full-to-empty range of 569 miles (915 km).

In time, a 400 V plug-in hybrid X5 50e xDrive will join the mix on the production line at Spartanburg, South Carolina, with a 26.5 kWh battery pack and about 44 miles (71 km) of electric range. And eventually, BMW’s hydrogen fuel cell tech will find its way under the hood of the new-generation X5 too. But those wanting something more efficient than the X5 40 can consider the iX5.

BMW is sticking with its strategy of an asynchronous motor for the front axle and an electrically excited synchronous motor for the rear drive unit, thanks to the lower losses of these motor types compared to motors that use permanent magnets. There is a combined output of 570 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft (804 Nm): The front motor generates 245 hp (183 kW) and 225 lb-ft (305 Nm); the rear produces up to 325 hp (242 kW) and 369 lb-ft (500 Nm).

Between the axles at the heart of the iX5 is a rather massive 144 kWh (usable) battery pack, made up of BMW’s new 120 mm cylindrical cells. These are taller than the 95 mm cells in the iX3, which increases energy density by 30 percent over the smaller SUV’s pack. So even if it’s not quite as long-legged as the gas X5, it should still get 450 miles (724 km) on the EPA test cycle, BMW told us. The car’s route planning is designed to take charging into account and uses onboard AI to “consider expected charging capacity, reliability, and precise station location data when selecting stops.” It will even automatically open the charging port flap when you arrive.

Like the smaller Neue Klasse EVs, the pack operates at 800 V, but it is even more capable when it comes to DC fast charging. At a demo during the first drive in California, we watched as an iX5 plugged in at 10 percent state of charge. Within a little over nine minutes, the EV had reached 50 percent SoC, peaking at 465 kW and averaging 375 kW throughout the session, which delivered 61.5 kWh. (The IONNA station had been specially upgraded to charge above the usual 400 kW.) While that kind of power level is now old hat for some Chinese automakers, it’s a big step forward for a European OEM.

A 10–80 percent fast charge takes as little as 22 minutes—provided you have access to a 460 kW charger—via the NACS port. That same port will accept up to 15.4 kW of AC power via BMW’s home charger, or you can use the provided 11 kW onboard AC charger. There are adapters for both V2H and V2L, as the X5 is capable of bidirectional charging.

No more dials

For decades, BMW’s orange-lit cluster of instrument dials was instantly recognizable. But the move to digital cockpit displays put an end to that. Now, the new HMI paradigm from Munich is the Panoramic Vision display, which blends into the windscreen’s frit ( the black border that’s painted on ). The display is clear and quite minimalist but very legible, appearing a few inches further down the hood and thus closer to where your eyes focus on the road than if you had to look down at a conventional dash. It first showed up in the iX3 and now arrives in the bigger X5. While it looks unfamiliar at first—and people sure seem to hate the unfamiliar these days—together with the full-color heads-up display, you rarely need to look down into the cockpit while driving.

That goes for interacting with the infotainment system, too. The trapezoidal touchscreen and BMW’s current iDrive OS user interface are easy to use, but the onboard personal assistant works much better than the Alexa-based system did last year in the early iX3 we drove. I recognize that I’m an outlier using voice commands to interact with the car, but when they work, I’m going to use them. Particularly in the absence of physical controls—“Hey BMW, turn on the driver’s seat massager” is easier for me to do behind the wheel than tapping the car icon to access vehicle settings and then scrolling down to seats and then selecting the tab for massage and then turning it on.

There’s also a passenger screen, although, helpfully, BMW made this its own option rather than including it in a package. The screen only allows the front seat passenger to watch streaming videos, play games, or browse the web—they cannot interact with native infotainment functions like navigation or the climate settings from that screen, just the one to its left.

The iX5 stops for red lights

Another difference between the gasoline X5 and the iX5 is that the latter features BMW’s new “ Heart of Joy .” This is one of the powerful domain controller computers that replaces the jumble of black boxes and single-function ECUs, in this case the one that manages vehicle dynamics. As we found with the iX3, this clever electronic brain enables solid chassis and powertrain control, including the ability to come to an incredibly smooth stop while one-pedal driving.

But the iX5 has another party trick that I didn’t notice in the smaller, cheaper EV: It will automatically detect red lights and stop signs, alerting you and braking the car if necessary (i.e., you were about to run the light or sign). The feature works whether you’ve engaged active drive assist or not. It’s always there like a safety net along with the car’s other advanced driver assistance systems. (I am sure you can disable this feature like the others, although I didn’t check, and I’m sure people will post comments with their particular edge case. Given driving standards these days, I’d be happier if everyone left it running.)

The new assist suite is called BMW Symbiotic Drive, and it’s of the very latest generation of ADAS that allows the driver to apply brake inputs without canceling out of active driving mode—only a heavy stomp on the brake will shut off cruise control.

The EV drives better

Neither X5 nor iX5 are unpleasant to drive. The X5’s engine is quiet, and neither car suffers from much wind noise. Unlike the iX, which had something of a “skyhook” magic carpet ride, both iX5 and X5 are more firmly sprung, but not bone-rattlingly so. But I give the edge to the heavier iX5—although the battery adds to a hefty 6,200 lb (2,813 kg) curb weight, the extra mass helps dampen the short-duration shocks that make it past the X5’s (optional) adaptive air suspension. Longer-duration bumps are smoothed out by either car.

If you have passengers in the iX5, you might find Sport mode has too violent an initial throttle tip-in; in the other throttle settings (eco, comfort), this is not an issue. The iX5 also offers five levels of lift-off regenerative braking, from none at all (it coasts very well) to 0.6 G of regen. And it has true one-pedal driving that will bring you to a complete stop.

The 2027 X5 40 xDrive starts at $72,100, plus a $1,450 delivery and handling charge, and you can already find them in BMW showrooms. There is still a premium for the electric version—144 kWh of lithium-ion isn’t cheap, after all. Thus, the iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800 plus delivery and arrives in Q1 2027.

stories.title: Samsung all but confirms iPhone Duo is goosing Galaxy Z8 sales
stories.summary: Searches for Samsung foldables just happened to skyrocket following iPhone Duo unveiling.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Searches for Samsung foldables just happened to skyrocket following iPhone Duo unveiling.

Android-powered foldable phones have been available for years, but most people never paid attention to them. As predicted, that could be changing now that Apple has entered the folding phone market with the iPhone Duo . Analysts have speculated that Samsung’s Z8 foldables were seeing a boost from the iPhone announcement, and now Samsung has seemingly confirmed that.

In a new blog post , Samsung UK crows that the company’s 2026 foldable lineup is moving much faster than last year’s models. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 7, combined European sales for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are up 45 percent. Samsung isn’t talking about Z Flip 8 sales, but it previously noted that its larger foldables made up about 80 percent of foldable purchases. We can assume any increase there is not impressive enough to mention.

The reason for flat Z Flip sales may simply be that Apple didn’t release a flip phone. Unsurprisingly, Samsung doesn’t mention Apple or the iPhone Duo in its press release. However, it does say that search volume for the Z8 series across Europe spiked 460 percent the week of September 6 to 12. And guess what was announced on September 9? Yep, the iPhone Duo. Z Fold 8 search volume across the entire month of September (when the phones launched) was up 260 percent.

Samsung noted last month that US preorders for the Galaxy Z8 series were trending 30 percent higher than last year, but it hasn’t confirmed any updated numbers for the US market. This meshes with third-party reports, which claimed Samsung was ramping up foldable manufacturing, particularly of the wider, iPhone-like Z Fold 8. The company isn’t talking about the proportion of Z Fold 8 versus Z Fold 8 Ultra sales, but it seems likely that Samsung’s wider foldable is doing better in the wake of Apple’s foldable announcement.

Are foldables cool now?

Samsung released its first foldable phone in 2019, and it was the only company seriously pursuing the form factor for several years. Those early devices were clunky and more interesting as feats of engineering than as things you’d want to carry around all day, but little by little, foldable hardware improved until Apple could finally release the product it wanted. The iPhone Duo is not an island—it relies on many of the same components as other foldable phones, including Samsung displays.

The Apple hype train is unstoppable, so increased interest in foldables was probably inevitable. Samsung expanded its foldable lineup with the non-Ultra model just in time, likely based on leaks of Apple’s device. But the wider form factor isn’t just a gimmick—it addresses several annoying issues with foldable phones. The main display is better for watching video with less wasted space. It’s also better for reading documents and using unoptimized apps (many of which are in the Play Store) in portrait orientation compared to square foldable screens. This is a positive change for foldable phones, and one we’ll probably see replicated by other OEMs in the coming months.

Regardless, foldable pricing is definitely not cool. It’s hard to justify spending $2,000 on a phone, but at the same time, all devices are getting more expensive. With recent price hikes, the top-end flat phones from Samsung, Google, and Apple are only a few hundred dollars away from their foldable options. Foldable prices have inched upward, too, but not by the same amount. Apple even managed an uncharacteristically competitive (for a foldable) price of $2,000 for the iPhone Duo. Samsung’s wide foldable is a little cheaper at $1,900, and it has been discounted at a few retailers since launch.

stories.title: EFF’s State Legislative Agenda to End ALPR Mass Surveillance
stories.summary: Police agencies across the U.S. have deployed Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) to capture images of passing vehicles along with time, date, and GPS coordinates. While the technology itself isn’t new (ALPRs have existed in various forms for more than 50 years , and in the U.S. since 1998 ), the surveillance landscape has shifted dramatically. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and national data sharing have transformed police ALPRs into an interconnected, nationwide tracking network. It is pitched to city councils by law enforcement and private vendors like Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), and Axon as an essential tool for solving violent crime. In reality, it is an inherently dangerous infrastructure of mass surveillance. Since 2012 , EFF has worked with others to expose the severe digital rights harms of ALPR systems. For example, we’ve recently documented how these camera networks allow law enforcement to search for immigrants , track peaceful protesters , target Romani communities , and track women seeking reproductive healthcare . Police also routinely use ALPRs for low-level matters like enforcing school residency requirements or investigating noise complaints . Many officers also use ALPR databases to stalk past romantic partners . Recent EFF analysis revealed officers using the system without legitimate justification—logging search reasons like "LOL" and "LMAO." Understandably, the public backlash to police ALPR technology is accelerating, and state lawmakers across the country are taking action. New Hampshire enacted the nation’s first state law on ALPR use in 2007, but technological advances and misconduct have driven even more recent legislative action. stories.title: EFF Launches Guide to Help Parents and Youth Protect Privacy Online
stories.summary: Guide Includes Easy, Quick Ways To Identify and Protect Against Online Threats SAN FRANCISCO – The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has published “ Online Privacy for Parents and Youth ,” a new guide to help families protect themselves online. "Parents don’t need to be technology experts to help their children navigate the digital world safely” said EFF Public Interest Technology Director Babette Ngene. “At EFF, we believe in empowering families with the knowledge and confidence to make informed decisions about their digital lives. It’s about meeting families where they are and giving parents the guidance they need to have meaningful conversations with their children about digital safety, based on what works best for their families.” EFF launches this crucial resource as state and local governments consider enacting well-meaning but ill-advised laws that cut young people off from essential information and experiences, particularly harming vulnerable youth and marginalized groups who often find safety in supportive online communities they can't access offline. Such laws also entail age gating, which compromises the privacy of all internet users and stifles young users’ ability to learn, grow, and express themselves. “Deciding how to help your young people use the internet—including engaging with video games, social media, web search, and everything else—is a complicated topic that touches on many different skillsets and ideas,” said EFF Senior Security and Privacy Activist Thorin Klosowski. “But ultimately it's up to families – not governments – to decide when and how to engage with these sorts of questions.” Each young person has unique needs, and, just like their wardrobe, that changes as they age. stories.title: Victory! Court Rules OPM Data Disclosure to DOGE Is Unlawful
stories.summary: In a victory for data privacy, a federal court in New York definitively ruled that the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) violated the law when it disclosed millions of federal employee records to DOGE agents. In a summary judgment ruling issued on October 20, 2026, the court found that OPM violated two provisions of the Privacy Act—one restricting disclosure of personal records between agencies and another requiring agencies to protect the security and confidentiality of records. Since the case was filed, many DOGE agents have left the government and OPM has rescinded their database access. However, OPM should still clean up the cybersecurity mess it created. The court will decide the remedy at a later date. "By virtue of the Court’s summary judgment ruling, OPM’s decision to grant DOGE Agents broad access to its systems of recordings containing [personally identifiable information (PII)] has been held unlawful," Judge Denise Cote wrote. "The record also provides no support for a finding that it was the pursuit of a modernization agenda that prompted OPM to grant sweeping and expedited access to a score of DOGE Agents to its systems of records containing PII," she added. OPM maintains databases of highly sensitive personal information about tens of millions of federal employees, retirees, and job applicants. Starting in January 2025, OPM disclosed data to the U.S. DOGE Service, initially led by Elon Musk. This disclosure violates the federal Privacy Act of 1974, a watershed anti-surveillance statute that prevents the federal government from abusing our personal information. EFF sued OPM and DOGE because this data disclosure violates the Privacy Act. We represent unions of federal employees – the American Federation of Government Employees and the Association of Administrative Law Judges – and individual employees. We seek injunctive and declaratory relief. We filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. Our co-counsel are Lex Lumina LLP , State Democracy Defenders Fund , and The Chandra Law Firm LLC . stories.title: The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information | Editorial
stories.summary: In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics Is there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases. It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future.
